quote: Nach {+Aufstellung+} einer vollstän- digen Molekularen Theorie besteht die Möglichkeit, dass man die physikalischen Constanten beseitigt (oder auf gewisse ganze rationale Zahlen, Anzahlen [-z-] zurückführt) so wie dies in der Geometrie bereits geschehen ist.
english: After the establishment of a complete molecular theory there is the possibility that one eliminates the physical constants (or reduces them to certain whole rational numbers, counts), just as has already happened in geometry.
topic: Methodological reflections: the lasting value of old theories, an analogy between the continuity axioms of geometry and molecular hypotheses in physics (including the possible elimination of physical constants), and arguments for the axiomatic method.

triage.modern_statement: This is not a precise mathematical problem. It is a methodological and physical conjecture: a complete atomic (molecular) theory of matter would let the dimensional constants of physics be eliminated, or derived as pure numbers such as integers or counts. Hilbert compares this to geometry, where the continuity axioms let measurement be reduced to counting. In modern terms it is close to two questions: whether the free parameters of fundamental physics can be cut down to dimensionless constants (natural units), and whether those dimensionless constants, such as the fine-structure constant α ≈ 1/137, can be derived from theory, possibly as rational or whole numbers. It belongs to the circle of ideas behind Hilbert's 6th problem (axiomatizing physics), but it is not itself one of the 23 problems.
triage.answered_by: Not answered. Arthur Eddington tried in the 1920s–30s to derive the inverse fine-structure constant as an integer (first 136, then 137), but the attempt failed: measurements show α is not exactly 1/137. Current theory, the Standard Model, cannot predict α or the other dimensionless constants; they still have to be measured. The part about dimensional constants is handled by choosing natural units, but the dimensionless pure numbers have not been reduced to integers or counts.

evidence.claim: The value of the fine-structure constant, a dimensionless quantity, cannot be predicted by theory; it is only measured.
Working out the fine-structure constant from theory has been called the most important unsolved problem of modern physics (as quoted in this paper).
Eddington argued that the inverse fine-structure constant was the whole number 136, later changing it to 137.
1/137 was once thought to be the exact value of the fine-structure constant, but it is not.
Hilbert's 6th problem asks for physics to be axiomatized on the model of geometry, and grew out of his own work on the foundations of geometry.

triage.why: Hilbert's remark is a speculative program, not a precise theorem. Its modern counterpart is well known and still open: no theory derives the dimensionless constants of physics, and attempts to make them whole numbers (Eddington's 137) failed. Work on the origin of the constants continues (Standard Model parameters, unification, string landscape debates), but the sources I found only directly confirm that α cannot be predicted and that Eddington's attempt failed. I am treating it as related to the 6th problem rather than identical to it. Confidence is medium because linking this short, informal note to the modern question involves interpretation; no source discusses this specific diary entry.
